Title: Are We Ready for the Metaverse? Implications, Legal Landscape, and Recommendations for Responsible Development

Abstract
The Metaverse, an interconnected, immersive, and persistent multi-user environ­
ment blending physical and digital realities, has transformative potential for society 
but also poses significant risks for individuals, businesses, and the environment. 
This study addresses the research gap in understanding these multifaceted implica­
tions by employing an integrated research approach. Initially, a literature review 
explores the opportunities and risks presented by the Metaverse. We then focus on 
risks to six sets of fundamental rights, analyzing existing legal standards and their 
applicability through doctrinal analysis and socio-legal research. The legal frame­
works included in this analysis are the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), 
the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, the Digital Services Act 
(DSA), and the EU AI Act (AIA). Finally, to mitigate identified risks, we provide 
dual-pronged recommendations that combine regulatory measures and technologi­
cal strategies. The study serves as a white paper, mapping the Metaverse landscape 
and providing actionable insights for policymakers, industry stakeholders, and tech­
nology developers. Our findings emphasize the need for a comprehensive approach 
that integrates robust regulatory frameworks with cutting-edge technical safeguards 
to ensure responsible and sustainable Metaverse development.

1  Introduction
The concept of the Metaverse, a network of interconnected, immersive, and persistent 
multi-user environments, blending physical reality with digital virtuality (Mourtzis 
et al., 2022), has sparked considerable attention. Distinct from merely virtual envi­
ronments and virtual reality (VR), which focuses primarily on simulated immersive 
interfaces, and digital twins, which replicate real-world assets, processes, or systems 
with real-time bi-directional data linkage, the Metaverse uniquely combines differ­
ent elements into “a continuum of physical and virtual systems, interconnected and 
intertwined in ways that allow for seamless transitions and interactions” (Tu et al., 
2024). While the European Union prefers the term “virtual world” to align with its 
values of digital sovereignty and inclusivity (Hupont et al., 2023), this paper adopts 
the term “Metaverse” to reflect its broader global recognition and resonance in aca­
demic and industry discourse. The Metaverse is powered by core technologies such 
as digital twins for seamless data flow, semantic models for knowledge synchroniza­
tion, extended reality (XR) for immersive user interactions, and support functions 
like Artificial Intelligence (AI) (Tu et al., 2021, 2022, 2024). The evolving role of 
Generative AI (GenAI) in the Metaverse is particularly significant, as it facilitates the 
creation of dynamic content, enhances user experiences, and automates various pro­
cesses. The Metaverse covers the consumer, enterprise, and industrial domains: The 
Consumer Metaverse focuses on entertainment and social interactions; the Enter­
prise Metaverse enhances business operations and collaboration; and the Industrial 
Metaverse revolutionizes manufacturing and logistics through advanced training, 
simulations and operations. As a limitless arena of exploration, interaction, and cre­
ation, the Metaverse promises potential applications as diverse and expansive as the 
user base it hopes to engage. From facilitating remote collaboration in virtual offices 
(Popescu et al., 2022), to offering immersive learning environments (Dahan et al., 
2022), enabling unique entertainment experiences (Niu & Feng, 2022), or revolu­
tionizing manufacturing operations by augmenting human workers with immersive 
data-driven insights (Tu et al., 2024), the Metaverse changes how we interact with 
digital content and with each other.
However, akin to any emerging technology, the Metaverse not only presents 
opportunities and benefits, but it also harbors the less discussed challenges and 
risks posed to individuals, businesses, and the environment. Previous research has 
highlighted the need for careful examination of the ethical, legal, and societal chal­
lenges to achieve an open, safe, and equitable Metaverse (Smith et al., 2023; Felice 
et al., 2023; Sami et al., 2023; Cheong, 2022). Studies have explored various sec­
tors impacted by the Metaverse, such as marketing, education, and healthcare, not­
ing issues related to social interaction, trust, privacy, bias, application of law, and 
the psychological impact on vulnerable populations (Dwivedi et al., 2022). Further, 
Giovanni (2023) has examined the economic, environmental, and social impacts of 
the Metaverse and connected them to the Sustainable Development Goals’ (SDGs) 
objectives and criteria. Tlili et al. (2023) have pointed out that more research should 
be conducted to provide a safe implementation of the Metaverse in industry.

The broad and multifaceted implications of the Metaverse remain largely unex­
plored, revealing a significant research gap that our paper seeks to address. Conse­
quently, our study poses research questions as follows:
1.	 What are the primary opportunities and risks associated with the Metaverse for 
individuals, businesses, and the environment?
2.	 How do existing legal standards apply to the unique context of the Metaverse?
3.	 What legal and technical measures are necessary to harness the transformative 
potential of the Metaverse while mitigating its inherent risks?
Addressing these research questions, our study employs an integrated research 
approach. We conduct a literature review to explore the opportunities and risks of the 
Metaverse and analyze existing legal frameworks to assess their adequacy through 
doctrinal analysis and socio-legal research. Based on these analysis, we incorporate 
technical, interdisciplinary, and applied research methods to propose recommenda­
tions. The study serves as a white paper aiming to map the Metaverse landscape and 
provide actionable insights for policy makers, industry stakeholders, and technology 
developers to ensure the responsible and sustainable development of the Metaverse. 
While the study does not aim to exhaustively address all potential opportunities, 
risks, legal standards, or recommendations, it focuses on key issues, contributing 
to the ongoing debate and referencing related sources that offer similar suggestions 
where applicable. In the legal analysis, we concentrate on the EU context due to its 
proactive regulatory stance, while recognizing the broad applicability of our find­
ings and recommendations to other jurisdictions, given the global and cross-juris­
dictional nature of the Metaverse. In sum, the study offers the following three key 
contributions:
1.	 An exploration of the opportunities and risks of the Metaverse for individuals, 
businesses, and the environment.
2.	 An analysis of existing legal standards and their applicability to the Metaverse.
3.	 Dual-pronged recommendations combining regulatory and technological mea­
sures to address the identified risks.
2  Methodology
To address the multifaceted nature of the Metaverse and provide comprehensive rec­
ommendations, our study employs an integrated research approach that combines 
elements of literature review, doctrinal analysis, socio-legal research, technical anal­
ysis, interdisciplinary analysis, and applied research. These methodologies jointly 
address the three research topics of this paper: the opportunities and risks of the 
Metaverse, the analysis of existing legal standards, as well as regulatory and techni­
cal recommendations, as illustrated in Fig. 1.
The literature review conducted for this study aims to explore and understand the 
opportunities and risks inherent in the Metaverse concept. A targeted and iterative 
approach is adopted to identify and analyze its diverse implication across multiple

3  Opportunities of the Metaverse
The emergence of the Metaverse is promising in reshaping how individuals interact, 
businesses operate, and environmental issues are addressed. This convergence of the 
digital and physical spaces introduces new experiences, communication avenues, and 
efficiencies that benefit diverse facets of society. This section explores the primary 
opportunities of the Metaverse on individuals, businesses, and the environment, as 
represented in Table 1.
3.1  Opportunities for Individuals
The Metaverse revolutionizes education by breaking down geographical barriers and 
democratizing access to diverse disciplines. Immersive language training, for exam­
ple, allows learners to practice in virtual environments that mimic real-world set­
tings, enhancing their understanding and retention (Wu et al., 2023). Enhanced social 
connectivity is another advantage conferred by the Metaverse, with the capacity to 
engage global communities via virtual gatherings (Bayram, 2022), as demonstrated 
by the World Economic Forum’s Global Collaboration Village (World Economic 
Forum, n.d.). Furthermore, the Metaverse facilitates a transformative approach to 
work-life balance, fostering remote and flexible work arrangements which can signif­
icantly reduce commute-associated stress (Bennett, 2022). Lastly, the Metaverse pro­
vides an expansive platform for creative expression (Lee et al., 2021a, b), enabling

3.2  Opportunities for Businesses
The Metaverse can strengthen collaboration and communication within teams, irre­
spective of their geographic distribution. Through virtual workspaces and immersive 
meetings, it fosters productivity and innovation while restraining travel necessities 
and associated costs (Bennett, 2022). Businesses are leveraging the Metaverse to 
generate new revenue streams through interactive virtual storefronts, immersive 
product try-ons, and the sale of virtual goods and non-fungible tokens (NFTs), as 
seen with Nike’s Nikeland on Roblox (Nike, n.d.). The Metaverse further allows for 
efficient supply chain management through real-time monitoring and optimization of 
operations (Queiroz et al., 2023), reducing waste and enabling proactive decision-
making, as demonstrated by Walmart’s use of IBM’s Food Trust blockchain platform 
(IBM, n.d.). Additionally, the Metaverse expedites prototyping and design, facili­
tating cost-effective product testing and refinement, leading to accelerated develop­
ment cycles and minimized time-to-market (Manuri, 2022), as illustrated by BMW’s 
use of virtual prototyping for their all-electric vehicle production line (BMW, 2020). 
Furthermore, the Metaverse offers efficient onboarding and training experiences and 
facilitates effective remote or augmented on-site operation of industrial processes (Tu 
et al., 2024), exemplified by platforms like NVIDIA’s Omniverse (NVIDIA, n.d.).
3.3  Opportunities for the Environment
The Metaverse can contribute to a smaller carbon footprint by minimizing the need 
for physical travel (Bennett, 2022), thereby reducing greenhouse gas emissions and 
strain on transportation infrastructure. For instance, the use of virtual conferences can 
reduce the carbon footprint by up to 94% compared to traditional in-person events 
(Tao et al., 2021). The capabilities of the Metaverse extend to reducing material 
waste and pollution through virtual prototyping (Manuri, 2022), leading to greater 
resource efficiency, as exemplified by Volkswagen’s Bugatti using VR for its car pro­
totype design (Ochanji, 2019). The Metaverse can enhance environmental awareness 
and advocacy via virtual simulations of environmental scenarios, thereby encourag­
ing sustainable practices (PwC, 2019). Furthermore, it serves as a platform for the 
research, development, and collaboration on sustainable technologies, accelerating 
the uptake of green solutions across industries (Liu et al., 2023). For instance, Sie­
mens and NVIDIA are leveraging the Industrial Metaverse to create real-time digital 
twins that improve operational efficiency and promote sustainable practices in manu­
facturing​ (Siemens, n.d.).

4  Risks of the Metaverse
The Metaverse, while offering numerous advantages, also presents risks. This section 
enumerates potential risks for individuals, businesses, and the environment in the 
context of the Metaverse, as represented in Table 2.
4.1  Risks for Individuals
The emergence of the Metaverse brings to the forefront the risk of personal data mis­
use, which may occur through theft, unauthorized resale, or illicit repurposing (Hine 
et al., 2024). Coupled with the collection, processing, analysis, and use of users’ 
biometric, behavioral, or genetic data, there is an increased potential for pervasive 
surveillance, posing a formidable threat to the right to privacy and the right to data 
protection. The extensive and personal nature of the data captured within the Meta­
verse means users’ most intimate and personal details could potentially be exposed 
or exploited (Wang et al., 2022).
Discrimination is another significant concern within the Metaverse. With the col­
lection of user information, ranging from basic demographic data such as gender, 
age, and ethnicity, to more intimate details like personal fears or interests, users could 
potentially face targeted discrimination (Han & Shi, 2024; Saka, 2023; Rosioru, 2023). 
Users could be singled out and manipulated based on their most private characteris­
tics, leading to gross violations of their right to equality and non-discrimination.
Digital identity, a fundamental element in the Metaverse, is fraught with risks. 
Issues of identity fraud and challenges related to authentication and verification pose 
significant threats to human dignity and self-determination. As users engage more 
with the Metaverse, their digital identities become increasingly valuable and, conse­
quently, attractive targets for fraudulent activities (Cheong, 2022).
The right to freedom of expression and information also faces unique chal­
lenges in the Metaverse. The pervasive use of AI can lead to deceptive representa­
tions, such as deep fakes or hacked avatars (Tariq et al., 2023). Additionally, the

4.2  Risks for Businesses
The Metaverse, while creating novel opportunities, also presents significant risks for 
businesses. Industrial espionage and intellectual property theft are among the 
most serious threats. Competitors or malicious actors may infiltrate the Metaverse to 
unlawfully acquire sensitive information, trade secrets, and proprietary designs. This 
potential exposure could lead to significant financial loss and damage to a company’s 
reputation, endangering its competitive position in the market (Kalyvaki, 2023).
Integration and compatibility represent another set of challenges within the 
Metaverse. The convergence of diverse platforms, systems, and devices may result in 
interoperability issues. These can manifest as inefficiencies, operational disruptions, 
or security vulnerabilities, thereby undermining the seamless functioning of business 
operations within the Metaverse (Gadekallu et al., 2023). This new, interconnected 
digital world demands an unprecedented level of integration and consistency to fully 
exploit its potential.
Competition and antitrust risks are critical concerns within the Metaverse, as 
its development could lead to the concentration of power among a few dominant 
players. These entities may control essential platforms, standards, or interoperability 
protocols (Massaro, 2024), creating barriers for smaller competitors and stifling inno­
vation. A monopolized Metaverse could result in reduced consumer choice, inflated 
prices, and potential misuse of market power, creating broader societal implications 
(Cagnina and Polan, 2008). In this scenario, businesses may face challenges such as 
limited access to critical technologies, increased dependency on dominant actors, 
and restricted interoperability, which could hinder their ability to operate effectively 
in the Metaverse (Nikalje, 2024). Addressing the balance of power and maintaining 
equitable market dynamics are essential for fostering healthy competition within this 
emerging digital environment.
Lastly, technical failures and security breaches present serious risks. Cyberat­
tacks or infrastructure failures within the Metaverse can disrupt operations, which 
can be especially damaging for businesses that rely heavily on real-time transac­
tions or services. Moreover, the resultant operational disruptions and downtime 
could adversely affect productivity and lead to substantial financial losses (Gupta et

4.3  Risks for the Environment
The environmental implications of the Metaverse are multifaceted, spanning from 
short-term to medium and long-term effects. A significant immediate concern is the 
energy consumption increase. The Metaverse’s dependence on data centers and 
high-performance computing for the generation and rendering of highly immer­
sive and resource-intensive virtual experiences can escalate energy consumption 
(Esposito et al., 2023). Furthermore, GenAI, a key enabler of the Metaverse, exacer­
bates this issue due to the substantial energy required for training and running Large 
Language Models (LLMs) and Large Vision Models (LVMs). Empirical data indi­
cates that training a single large AI model can emit as much carbon dioxide as five 
passenger vehicles over their lifespans (Strubell et al., 2019). This increase may in 
turn lead to a surge in greenhouse gas emissions, contrary to global efforts to reduce 
carbon footprints and mitigate climate change.
In the medium to long term, the rapid increase of devices and hardware necessary 
for Metaverse access, such as XR headsets and advanced computing hardware, raises 
concerns about electronic waste, often referred to as e-waste (Esposito et al., 2023). 
The Global E-waste Monitor 2020 (Forti et al., 2020) reported that the world gener­
ated 53.6 million metric tons of e-waste in 2019, a figure projected to rise to 74.7 mil­
lion metric tons by 2030, nearly doubling in just 16 years. The expansion of the 
Metaverse is anticipated to exacerbate this trend, contributing to the growing global 
e-waste challenge. E-waste presents not only environmental hazards, as electronic 
components often contain toxic substances, but also health risks to those involved in 
the disposal and recycling of these devices.
Another long-term impact is the potential exacerbation of the digital divide over 
time. The Metaverse’s dependency on high-speed internet and cutting-edge tech­
nologies may widen socio-economic disparities, particularly in regions with limited 
resources and infrastructure (Bibri, 2022). This divide could hinder equitable access 
and sustainable development, creating a digital exclusivity that marginalizes under­
served populations.
5  Analysis of the Existing Legal Standards
Given the unique nature of the Metaverse and the new dimensions it adds to interac­
tions and experiences in society, existing legal standards must be applied and inter­
preted to address emerging risks to people’s rights effectively. This section analyzes 
key legal standards in the context of the Metaverse, focusing on risks to the six sets 
of fundamental rights identified in the previous section: (1) privacy and data protec­
tion; (2) equality and non-discrimination; (3) digital identity, human autonomy, and 
self-determination; (4) freedom of expression and information; (5) fair and just work­
ing conditions; (6) physical and mental integrity. This paper examines the Charter

Protection Regulation (GDPR) (Regulation (EU), 2016), the Digital Services Act 
(DSA) (Regulation (EU), 2022), and the EU AI Act (AIA) (Regulation (EU), 2024).
The Charter is particularly applicable as it establishes a broad range of civil, polit­
ical, economic, and social rights that are applicable to individuals within the EU, and 
these rights extend into the digital domain, including the Metaverse. This includes, 
but is not limited to, respect for private and family life, protection of personal data, 
freedom of expression and information, and the prohibition of discrimination.
The GDPR is crucial as it provides a comprehensive framework for data protec­
tion, a significant concern in the Metaverse due to the complex and often sensitive 
personal data involved. The GDPR safeguards users’ rights to privacy and control 
over their personal information, a central requirement in the interconnected virtual 
worlds of the Metaverse.
The DSA is expected to play a key role, especially given the probable significance 
of Very Large Online Platforms (VLOPs) in hosting and operating the Metaverse. 
The DSA sets standards for transparency, accountability, and user empowerment for 
these platforms, and these principles will be paramount in ensuring a secure and user-
centered Metaverse experience.
Lastly, some of the risks explored above are connected to the evolving role of the 
AI module, especially GenAI, in the Metaverse. Therefore, it is relevant to under­
stand how the AIA will be applied in the context of the Metaverse, according to the 
specific intended purpose and risk categorisation of AI systems in the Metaverse 
architecture.
5.1  Privacy and Data Protection
The identified threats to the right to privacy and the right to data protection in the 
Metaverse are already subjected to existing legal safeguards. Starting from the Char­
ter, which guarantees that every individual has the right to respect for his or her 
private life (Article 7) and the right to protection of personal data concerning him 
or her (Article 8), including the right to access the data collected, the right to have it 
rectified, and the need for consent and legitimate data processing. These fundamental 
rights must be fully respected in the virtual worlds in the same way as in the physical 
world.
The legal framework that protects personal data more specifically in the EU is 
the GDPR. The applicability of the GDPR in the Metaverse is crucial for preventing 
and mitigating the significant data protection risks identified in this study. Article 6 
describes the requirements for the lawful processing of personal data; and Article 9 
prohibits the processing of special categories of personal data, except in the cases 
described in paragraph 2. These provisions are of fundamental importance in the 
context of the Metaverse, especially considering the unprecedented level of collec­
tion of individuals’ biometric, behavioral, or genetic data. The tailored interpretation 
and enforcement of Article 9 in virtual worlds will be key measures for the effective 
protection of users’ rights.
The recently adopted DSA will play a fundamental role in protecting the rights to 
privacy and data protection of users in the Metaverse. Article 34 imposes on provid­

Apart from the abovementioned legal provisions, when it comes to privacy and 
data protection, the AIA aims to facilitate the effective implementation of data pro­
tection under Union law (Recital 10). This regulation does not seek to affect the 
application of the GDPR, on the contrary, this legal regime ought to reinforce data 
protection. Recital 69 consolidates that legislative goal, stating that “the right to pri­
vacy and to protection of personal data must be guaranteed throughout the entire 
lifecycle of the AI system”. In this regard, the principles of data minimisation and 
data protection by design and by default, as set out in Union data protection law, are 
applicable when personal data are processed in the development or deployment of AI 
systems. More concretely, measures taken by providers to ensure compliance with 
those principles may include not only anonymization and encryption, but also the 
use of technology that permits algorithms to be brought to the data and allows train­
ing of AI systems without the transmission between parties or copying of the raw or 
structured data themselves. Apart from these general provisions, depending on the 
intended purpose and context of use of AI in the metaverse, some AI systems can be 
considered high-risk according to the AIA. In these cases, the Act imposes several 
requirements that must be observed, including Data Governance requirements (Arti­
cle 10, AIA), with specific rules on processing of special categories of personal data 
(Article 10(5), AIA). These requirements will have an even more direct contribution 
to respecting privacy and data protection when high-risk AI systems are part of the 
Metaverse architecture.
5.2  Equality and Non-Discrimination
Due to the unprecedented level of collection of data revealing racial or ethnic ori­
gin, gender, sexual orientation, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, 
trade union membership, among other personal and sensitive characteristics; and 
the processing of biometric, behavioral, or genetic data, the risks of discriminatory 
outcomes in the Metaverse cannot be ignored. Notwithstanding, existing EU laws 
already protect individuals against these risks, and they must be observed in the vir­
tual worlds to prevent targeted discrimination, profiling, social scoring, bullying, and 
harassment, among other issues.
The rights to equality and non-discrimination (Articles 20 and 21, the Charter) are 
the fundamental protection of individuals against this backdrop. These rights must be 
actively protected and fulfilled in the Metaverse, and their interpretation should be 
tailored to the new and improved threats that virtual worlds’ ecosystems entail.
Similarly, as previously stated, GDPR’s Article 9 plays a crucial role in the Meta­
verse. The prohibition of processing of special categories of personal data, as defined 
by the EU’s most relevant data protection law, (with the exception of the prescribed 
conditions in paragraph 2), must be implemented within the entire ecosystem of 
the Metaverse to prevent harm to user’s right to equality and non-discrimination.

Furthermore, the processing of large amounts of special personal data creates unique 
profiles of the individual users in the Metaverse, which might also be used for auto­
mated decision-making (Article 22, GDPR) and/or profiling (Article 4(4), GDPR), 
which can create and perpetuate existing stereotypes and social segregation.
The profiling of individuals based on special categories of personal data can also 
be used for target advertising in the Metaverse, which is prohibited by Article 26, 
paragraph 3 of the DSA. In the same context, Article 39 of the DSA imposes addi­
tional rules for online advertising transparency. Moreover, DSA’s Article 34 imposes 
on VLOPs the obligation to carry out risk assessments in order to identify any actual 
or foreseeable negative effects on the exercise of fundamental rights.
Additional protection to people’s right to non-discrimination in this context will be 
provided by the AIA’s prohibition on “AI systems evaluating or classifying people on 
the basis of multiple data points related to their social behaviour or known, inferred 
or predicted personal or personality characteristics, leading to detrimental or unfa­
vourable treatment of certain natural persons or groups of persons”, which the EU 
legislator calls AI systems providing social scoring (Article 5 (1)(c), AIA).
The compliance with and monitoring of these legal safeguards in the Metaverse 
will be challenging. Metaverse platforms and third parties must observe these obli­
gations taking into account the asymmetries of information and power imbalances 
between themselves and users in order to meaningfully and effectively protect peo­
ple’s fundamental rights.
5.3  Digital Identity, Human Dignity, and Self-Determination
The diverse suite of technologies underpinning the Metaverse inherently brings 
forth both new challenges and magnifies existing ones concerning individual rights. 
Among these, the risk of identity theft, alongside other cybersecurity threats such 
as hacking, malware, denial-of-service attacks, as well as various forms of fraud 
and phishing scams, command significant attention. The concept of digital identity 
remains paramount within these virtual realms. Consequently, any risks impinging 
upon identity, authentication, and verification processes threaten not only the security 
of users but also their dignity and self-determination.
To protect users against these harms, Metaverse operators must observe Article 1 
of the Charter, which safeguards human dignity. Our identity, physical and virtual, 
in both physical and virtual worlds, is intrinsically connected to our human dignity. 
Human dignity captures the notion that every human being is unique and valuable, 
and, therefore, entitled to human rights. Therefore, the protection and preservation of 
one’s identity is crucial in the Metaverse.
Another important legal safeguard that aims at protecting human dignity is defined 
by DSA’s Recital 67, Article 25, and Article 31, regarding the prohibition of dark 
patterns. Dark patterns are described as practices of deceiving or nudging users and 
distorting or impairing their autonomy, decision-making, or choice. As already men­
tioned, DSA’s Article 34, states that VLOPs must carry out risk assessments to iden­
tify any actual or foreseeable negative effects on the exercise of fundamental rights. 
This requirement, if effectively observed, will be an essential safeguard of human 
autonomy and dignity.

5.4  Freedom of Expression and Information
Misinformation is one of the biggest challenges in the era of digitalization and AI. 
To mitigate this problem in the Metaverse, the fundamental right to freedom of 
expression and information (Article 11, the Charter) must be respected. There is an 
urgent need to reinterpret this right in light of the technological ecosystem within the 
Metaverse.
VLOPs hosting and operating in the Metaverse will face an unprecedented chal­
lenge in preventing the spread of misinformation in virtual worlds, considering the 
new and augmented issues brought or exacerbated by AI and especially GenAI, such 
as deep fakes and hacked avatars. To achieve that goal, these actors must comply 
with the requirement of risk assessment to identify any actual or foreseeable negative 
effects for the exercise of fundamental rights (Article 34, DSA), including the right to 
freedom of expression and information.
Article 50 of the AIA will also impose important obligations to prevent the risks 
of misinformation and manipulation powered by AI in the Metaverse. This provi­
sion imposes transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI sys­
tems and General-purpose AI (GPAI) models. When people interact directly with AI 
systems in the Metaverse, they must be informed of this interaction, except when 
those systems are permitted by law to detect, prevent or investigate criminal offences 
(Article 50(1), AIA). Synthetic audio, image, video, or text generated by GPAI sys­
tems shall be marked in a machine-readable format and disclosed as AI generated 
(Article 50(2)(4), AIA). Finally, when an emotion recognition system or a biometric 
categorisation system is part of the AI module, users of the Metaverse exposed to the 
operation of the system must be informed, except when those systems are permitted 
by law to detect, prevent or investigate criminal offences (Article 50(3), AIA).
5.5  Fair and Just Working Conditions
The risk of workplace surveillance will be exponentially higher in the Metaverse. 
To avoid this harm, the right to privacy (Article 7, the Charter) and the right to 
protection of personal data (Article 8, the Charter) must be interpreted, applied, and 
monitored considering the unprecedented level of personal and non-personal data 
collected in the Metaverse, especially special categories of personal data. Moreover, 
in the context of the Enterprise Metaverse and the Industrial Metaverse, the right to 
engage in work (Article 15, the Charter) and the right to fair and just working condi­
tions (Article 31, the Charter) will require a tailored implementation as well. In order

5.6  Physical and Mental Integrity
The right to the integrity of the person (Article 3, the Charter) will apply in virtual 
worlds in the same way it applies to the physical world. Research has shown that 
harms to avatars brought by harassment, bullying, and other forms of exploitation and 
psychological violence can be as harmful as they are in the physical world (Dwivedi 
et al., 2023). All actors in the Metaverse must respect the right to the integrity of all 
persons in the virtual world.
In the same way, Article 9 of the DSA requires VLOPs to act against illegal con­
tent and behavior on online platforms. This is already a big challenge for these actors 
which will be exacerbated with the emerging Metaverse. The additional requirement 
from the DSA’s Article 34 reinforces this legal protection, by requiring risk assess­
ment to identify any actual or foreseeable negative effects for the exercise of funda­
mental rights.
With the power of GenAI, the harms of harassment, bullying and any other form of 
exploitation and psychological violence in the Metaverse can be significantly exac­
erbated. Research has identified that one of the most significant risks of GenAI in the 
Metaverse is large-scale toxic and harmful content generation (Wang et al., 2024; 
van der Sloot, 2024). If malicious actors in the Metaverse leverage the power of 
GenAI to harm the physical and mental integrity of users using harmful and toxic 
synthetic text, images, audios, and videos, suddenly, this risk arises to an unforesee­
able scale. The AIA will play a key role in addressing these problems and prevent­
ing harm to people’s physical and mental integrity through AI-enabled harassment 
and toxic behaviour. GPAI models’ providers must comply with specific obligations 
under Article 53, AIA.
If the AI model is considered as posing a systemic risk, which means models that 
can greatly influence the internal market because of their extensive scope, or are rea­
sonably likely to negatively impact public health, safety, security, fundamental rights, 
or society at large; they are subject to stricter requirements than other GPAI models. 
The providers of such models must perform model evaluation, assess and mitigate 
possible systemic risks, report serious incidents to the AI Office, and ensure adequate 
level of cybersecurity and and the physical infrastructure of the model (Article 55, 
AIA). Lastly, synthetic audio, image, video, or text generated by GPAI systems shall

6  Recommendations: Addressing Regulatory Gaps and Advancing 
Technical Measures
This section proposes recommendations to counter the risks inherent to the Meta­
verse. This includes both the deployment of robust regulatory measures to fill exist­
ing legal and policy gaps and the advancement of technical safeguards, targeting 
three primary categories: individual, business, and environmental risks.
6.1  Addressing Risks for Individuals
Given the delicate nature of the risks involved, it is crucial to establish a robust regu­
latory framework to safeguard users’ rights and interests in the Metaverse. Policy­
makers and regulators should ensure that the fundamental rights of Metaverse users 
are effectively respected in these immersive environments. In this regard, we propose 
the following regulatory recommendations.
All actors involved in the collection, processing, analysis, and use of data in the 
Metaverse should be required to carry out Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment 
(including data protection impact assessment), as part of human rights and environ­
mental due diligence processes. Privacy-preserving tools, mechanisms, and processes 
must be present since the beginning of the technologies’ lifecycles. Special protection 
must be provided for biometric, behavioral, and genetic data. The invasiveness of 
their collection at scale will entail an unprecedented risk to the right to privacy and 
other fundamental rights, once sensitive inferences could be made about individuals’ 
most intimate attributes such as preferences, fears, and feelings. Biometric, behav­
ioral, and genetic data could be not only exploited by virtual world enterprises but 
they could be sold to third parties causing extreme harm to users.
Second, with the rapid advent of GenAI and its disruptive nature, the safeguards 
imposed by current digital laws in the EU might not be sufficient to protect individu­
als in the Metaverse. One example is the disclosure of deepfakes required by the AIA 
(Article 50(4)), which might not be sufficient to ensure transparency and avoid users’ 
manipulation in the immersive experience of the Metaverse.
Moreover, robust governance frameworks should ensure that the use of Metaverse 
technologies is ethical and aligned with human rights. Regulatory requirements shall 
aim at preventing the use of surveillance and profiling technologies, and unfair and 
biased algorithms that discriminate against individuals based on their personal and 
most intimate characteristics.
While regulation and policy changes are a crucial part of addressing these chal­
lenges, technological advancements and improvements are equally important. In this 
regard, we present a set of recommendations to enhance the technical robustness of 
the Metaverse as follows.

6.1.1  Data Privacy and Protection Breaches
To prevent and mitigate the risk to data privacy and protection, we suggest techno­
logical measures such as the use of end-to-end encryption and secure communication 
protocols (Di Pietro & Cresci, 2021) to prevent unauthorized access to personal data 
and communication. Strong authentication mechanisms, such as biometric or multi-
factor authentication to ensure that only authorized users can access personal data 
(Kürtünlüoğlu et al., 2022), will also play an important role, as well as the use of 
decentralized identity systems (Ryu et al., 2022) that give users control over their per­
sonal data and allow them to share it only with trusted entities. To enhance privacy-
preserving technologies (Chen et al., 2023), the application of differential privacy 
can ensure the anonymization of individual data points while enabling aggregate data 
analysis for insights without compromising user privacy (Letafati & Otoum, 2023). 
In the Metaverse, differential privacy algorithms can be used to personalize advertis­
ing without user profiling or crowdsource world-building insights. Moreover, secure 
multiparty computation (SMPC) could be deployed in scenarios requiring collabora­
tive data analysis without sharing sensitive raw data (Jang et al., 2024). For instance, 
SMPC could enable multiple entities within the Metaverse to jointly train AI models 
on user data without exposing the underlying datasets to each other.
6.1.2  Threats to Equality and Non-Discrimination
Technological measures must be in place to prevent discrimination in virtual worlds, 
including the development of fair and unbiased algorithms (Kaur et al., 2021) that do 
not discriminate based on characteristics such as gender, race, or age. Additionally, 
the use of explainable AI (Gunning et al., 2019) is crucial to ensure that algorithmic 
decision-making is understandable and transparent and can be audited for discrimina­
tory outcomes. Lastly, a collection of diverse and inclusive datasets (Chi et al., 2021) 
that cover a range of demographic groups to avoid reinforcing biases must be at the 
core of Metaverse technologies.
6.1.3  Threats to Digital Identity, Human Dignity, and Self-Determination
To prevent these harms to Metaverse users’ digital identity, human dignity, and self-
determination, we suggest technological measures such as leveraging blockchain 
technology for secure and decentralized storage of digital identity information (Tao 
et al., 2023), which can prevent fraud and provide users with control over their per­
sonal data. Other important technological measures to mitigate these risks are open 
standards and interoperability frameworks to prevent vendor lock-in and give users 
the freedom to switch between virtual worlds or platforms as they choose (Lombardi 
& Lombardi, 2010; Awadallah et al., 2023). The integration of self-sovereign identity 
(SSI) empowers users to manage digital identities independently, enhancing privacy 
through cryptographically secure credentials (Ghirmai et al., 2022). Finally, Meta­
verse enterprises must implement user-centric design principles that prioritize user 
control over their virtual environment and avatars (Lee et al., 2021a, b).

6.1.4  Suppression of Freedom of Expression and Information
To mitigate the risk to freedom of expression and information, Metaverse enter­
prises should develop advanced authentication and verification techniques to prevent 
deep fake or hacked avatar-based attacks on their platform (Tariq et al., 2023). The 
use of blockchain or other decentralized technologies will contribute to creating a 
trusted source of information in the virtual world (Kumar & Sharma, 2022). Also, 
the development of AI-based tools for content analysis and classification (Demartini 
et al., 2020) will help identify potentially harmful or misleading content. Emerging 
technologies like quantum computing could further enhance security by providing 
advanced encryption methods resistant to brute-force attacks, ensuring secure com­
munication channels and data integrity within the Metaverse. Quantum key distribu­
tion (QKD), for instance, could offer an unbreakable way to share encryption keys, 
safeguarding sensitive information and interactions in virtual environments (Kumar 
et al., 2024).
6.1.5  Erosion of Fair and Just Working Conditions
In the Metaverse, workers will have data collected on them at an unprecedented level, 
it is crucial that corporations are required to implement privacy-by-design principles 
(Schaar, 2010) to ensure that workers’ data is only collected when necessary, and 
kept secure and confidential. Although the use of wearable technology and Internet 
of Things (IoT) devices to monitor workers’ safety and well-being can bring positive 
outcomes and benefit workers, there must be clear policies and protocols in place for 
how the data will be collected, used, and stored (Lim et al., 2022). Finally, explain­
able AI systems will help ensure that algorithmic decision-making in the workplace 
is transparent and understandable to workers (Taj & Zaman, 2022).
6.1.6  Harms to Physical and Mental Integrity
Robust content moderation employing machine learning and human expertise (Gil­
lespie, 2020) can help swiftly identify harmful content. User control over their 
experiences (Lewis & Rosie, 2012), such as the ability to block other users or mute 
conversations, should be prioritized, while personal space protection mechanisms 
(Nassiri et al., 2010) can prevent unwanted intrusions. Furthermore, by working 
closely with mental health professionals, Metaverse platforms can develop systems 
to provide immediate assistance for users encountering distressing situations, thus 
strengthening user safety and overall Metaverse integrity.
6.2  Addressing Risks for Businesses
This section provides detailed recommendations for addressing business risks in the 
Metaverse, including industrial espionage and intellectual property theft, integration 
and compatibility issues, and technical failures and security breaches, leveraging a 
comprehensive approach combining regulatory and technical measures.

6.2.1  Industrial Espionage and Intellectual Property Theft
Regulatory measures should be established to protect intellectual property rights 
within the Metaverse. The EU regulator should clarify the rights and obligations 
of all actors involved in the Metaverse regarding intellectual property. The right to 
intellectual property must be equally protected in physical and virtual worlds. Cor­
porations and individuals, for example, creators, must have the rights to their work, 
inventions, and creations sufficiently protected. Appropriate cybersecurity policies 
and governance are also needed to prevent industrial espionage. Policymakers and 
regulators should implement robust cybersecurity obligations for Metaverse enter­
prises, including regular security updates, and employee training, to protect against 
these risks. On the technological front, Metaverse entities should employ role-based 
access control (RBAC) systems to limit access to sensitive information based on 
user roles and responsibilities (Saxena & Alam, 2023). Digital Rights Management 
(DRM) systems can help protect proprietary digital assets and monitor their usage 
within the Metaverse (Subramanya & Yi, 2006). Additionally, the use of intrusion 
detection and prevention systems (IDPS) can ensure real-time responses to unauthor­
ized access attempts or unusual activities (Scarfone & Mell, 2007).
6.2.2  Integration and Compatibility Issues
To manage integration and compatibility risks, we suggest a robust, responsible, and 
multistakeholder governance framework for the Metaverse, which will contribute to 
steering standardization efforts and better interoperability between different Meta­
verse instances within the broader Metaverse ecosystem. We recommend that the 
present EU initiative encourages the adoption of industry standards and protocols 
to ensure seamless interoperability and compatibility across different platforms, 
devices, and systems. Technological solutions should also be pursued. Metaverse 
enterprises should perform extensive testing and validation during the development 
and integration phases to identify and resolve potential compatibility issues and vul­
nerabilities (Wang et al., 2022). Finally, a modular and scalable design approach 
(Jaynes et al., 2003; Tu et al., 2024) should be adopted to facilitate the integration 
of new technologies or upgrades without disrupting existing systems and processes.
6.2.3  Competition and Antitrust Risks
To address competition and antitrust risks in the Metaverse, regulatory measures 
must ensure fair market dynamics and prevent monopolistic practices. EU regula­
tors should interpret and enforce antitrust laws in the context of the Metaverse, such 
as Articles 101 and 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union 
(TFEU), to deter anti-competitive behaviors like market monopolization, price-
fixing, and abuse of dominant positions (Massaro, 2024). The Digital Markets Act 
(DMA) should play a critical role by imposing obligations on gatekeepers to foster 
competition and transparency in platform ecosystems (Massaro, 2024). Clear guide­
lines on the fair allocation of digital resources, such as virtual land and assets, can 
also prevent concentration of power among a few dominant players. On the techno­

6.2.4  Technical Failures and Security Breaches
Stringent cybersecurity regulation and governance frameworks should be established, 
enabling innovation while ensuring online protection for users and content creators in 
the Metaverse. Technologically, implementing redundant systems and backup strate­

outages (Liu et al., 2016). However, redundant systems demand significant financial 
investment in hardware, software, and infrastructure, posing challenges for smaller 
companies with limited budgets. As the Metaverse scales, their cost and complexity 
can grow exponentially, widening the competitive gap with larger corporations. Busi­
nesses may consider leveraging cloud-based redundancy solutions, which can offer 
scalable and cost-efficient alternatives to traditional on-premises systems. Robust 
cybersecurity measures including firewalls, regular security updates, and employee 
training can protect against cyber threats. Additionally, continuous monitoring of 
Metaverse infrastructure, coupled with regular maintenance and updates, can pre­
empt potential issues and optimize performance.
6.3  Addressing Risks for the Environment
This section outlines strategies to mitigate environmental risks in the Metaverse, 
from short-term to medium and long-term risks, including energy consumption, elec­
tronic waste, and the digital divide, through both regulatory and technical measures.
6.3.1  Energy Consumption Increase
To tackle immediate energy concerns, EU regulators should encourage the devel­
opment of the Metaverse ecosystem in alignment with the 2030 Agenda for the 17 
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the EU’s carbon neutrality objectives. 
The Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) further emphasizes 
the importance of corporate accountability in identifying, preventing, and mitigating 
adverse environmental impacts across supply chains (Schall, 2024). For Metaverse 
companies, this should include performing due diligence on the energy efficiency 
of data centers and the environmental impact of Metaverse platforms and services. 
Focusing on the environmental impact of AI systems, the AIA addresses the envi­
ronmental impacts of AI systems. Starting from the purpose of the regulation, the 
EU legislator affirms that the AIA aims to ensure a high level of protection of health, 
safety, fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including environmental protec­
tion, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union (Article 1, AIA). Due

and software solutions can mitigate energy consumption. Efficient cooling systems, 
renewable energy sources, and advanced power management systems in data centers 
can contribute substantially to this goal. Edge computing can distribute processing 
power closer to end-users, reducing the load on centralized data centers and curbing 
energy consumption (Zhang et al., 2023). Furthermore, energy-efficient rendering 
techniques and algorithms can minimize the environmental impact of virtual experi­
ences. Particularly, optimizing GenAI models used in the Metaverse to minimize 
computational costs and enhancing carbon efficiency can alleviate their energy inten­
sity (Li et al., 2024).
6.3.2  Electronic Waste
Mitigating the medium to long-term accumulation of e-waste requires a holis­
tic approach involving sustainable governance models and compliance with the 
CSDDD’s provisions. This directive calls on companies to ensure responsible 
sourcing of raw materials and lifecycle management of their products, emphasizing 
extended producer responsibility. In addition, the forthcoming Digital Product Pass­
port (DPP) under the EU’s Circular Economy Action Plan (CEAP) aims to enhance 
transparency regarding a product’s environmental impact throughout its lifecycle 
(Spani, 2020). Companies developing Metaverse-related hardware and devices will 
need to embed the DPP to provide information on energy efficiency, repairability, and 
recyclability, ensuring that their products meet sustainability benchmarks. Further­
more, AI sustainability standards under development in Europe may include specific 
metrics for assessing the environmental footprint of hardware supporting AI-driven 
systems (Perucica & Andjelkovic, 2022), ensuring that Metaverse devices adhere to 
strict sustainability criteria. Technical solutions also play a crucial role. Encouraging 
Metaverse enterprises to adopt modular and upgradable hardware designs can pro­
long the lifespan of devices, reducing e-waste (Kshetri & Dwivedi, 2023). The use

7  Conclusion
This white paper explores the multifaceted implications of the Metaverse for indi­
viduals, businesses, and the environment, mapping the Metaverse landscape and pro­
viding actionable insights for policymakers, industry stakeholders, and technology 
developers. Leveraging an integrated research approach, the paper (1) presents the 
primary opportunities and risks, (2) analyzes existing legal standards and their appli­
cability against the identified risks to the six sets of fundamental rights, as well as 
(3) recommends regulatory and technical measures for a responsible and sustainable 
Metaverse development. The key findings for the three aspects are summarized as 
follows.
7.1  Opportunities and risks 
The Metaverse offers transformative potential across various domains. For indi­
viduals, it democratizes education, enhances social connections, promotes health­
ier work-life integration, and provides a platform for creativity. Businesses benefit 
from improved remote collaboration, new revenue streams, efficient supply chains, 
enhanced onboarding and training, effective industrial operations, and accelerated 
development cycles. Environmentally, it helps reduce carbon footprints, minimize 
material waste, raise environmental awareness, and promote sustainable technolo­
gies. Meanwhile, the Metaverse also surfaces significant risks. Individuals face 
threats to the right to privacy and data protection, equality and non-discrimination, 
digital identity, human dignity and self-determination, freedom of expression and 
information, the right to fair and just working conditions, as well as physical and 
mental integrity. Similarly, businesses encounter potential industrial espionage and 
intellectual property theft, integration and compatibility issues, competition and anti­
trust risks, as well as technical failures and security breaches. Additionally, environ­
mental concerns arise from increased energy consumption, electronic waste, and a 
potentially exacerbated digital divide.

7.2  Existing Legal Standards
This paper analyzes the applicability of current legal standards with respect to the 
identified risks to six sets of fundamental rights of individuals in the Metaverse: The 
Charter ensures, among other rights, respect for private and family life, protection of 
personal data, freedom of expression, and prohibition of discrimination, all of which 
need reinterpretation and enforcement within this digital space; The GDPR’s frame­
work for lawful processing, consent, and data minimization is crucial for protecting 
user privacy in the complex data environment of the Metaverse; The DSA imposes 
standards for transparency, accountability, and user empowerment, particularly for 
VLOPs operating in the Metaverse, and mandates risk assessments to safeguard fun­
damental rights; The AIA regulates AI systems to prevent manipulative or biased 
algorithms from undermining fundamental rights, requiring transparency, robust data 
governance, and prohibiting AI applications posing unacceptable risks, which are 
increasingly important with the evolving role of GenAI in the Metaverse. While these 
legal standards are essential, they might not be sufficient in their current form, neces­
sitating a thorough reinterpretation and tailored implementation to align them with 
the unique needs of the Metaverse. Future research could deepen the exploration of 
how these frameworks intersect and how they reinforce each other, such as the poten­
tial overlap between the DSA’s platform accountability provisions and the GDPR’s 
data protection obligations, to identify areas where additional regulatory clarification 
may be needed. Additionally, investigating ethical AI frameworks and their role in 
responsible AI deployment within the Metaverse is a crucial area for further study. 
While this paper focuses on EU legal frameworks, we acknowledge the global nature 
of the Metaverse and the importance of cross-jurisdictional harmonization. Compara­
tive legal analyses across jurisdictions such as the US and China, alongside ongoing 
efforts by international regulatory bodies like the International Telecommunication 
Union (ITU)’s work on digital standards, and industry-focused initiatives like the 
World Economic Forum’s Global Future Council on the Metaverse, would provide 
valuable insights for fostering a coherent global regulatory landscape.
7.3  Recommendations
Based on the identified risks and existing legal standard analysis, this paper proposes 
recommendations including robust regulatory frameworks and technical safeguards 
across individual, business, and environmental domains. For individuals, we advo­
cate for Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments, enhanced data privacy, and pro­
tection mechanisms, alongside technologies like decentralized identity systems and 
privacy-preserving AI techniques. For businesses, we suggest regulatory measures 
to protect intellectual property, address competition risks, enforce cybersecurity, and 
ensure interoperability, reinforced by technical solutions like role-based access con­
trols and modular system designs. On the environmental front, strategies align with 
EU sustainability goals, focusing on energy-efficient AI and Metaverse development, 
sustainable e-waste management, and expanding broadband to bridge the digital 
divide.

Abstract: The Metaverse, an interconnected, immersive, and persistent multi-user environ­ ment blending physical and digital realities, has transformative potential for society but also poses significant risks for individuals, businesses, and the environment. This study addresses the research gap in understanding these multifaceted implica­ tions by employing an integrated research approach. Initially, a literature review explores the opportunities and risks presented by the Metaverse. We then focus on risks to six sets of fundamental rights, analyzing existing legal standards and their applicability through doctrinal analysis and socio-legal research. The legal frame­ works included in this analysis are the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, the Digital Services Act (DSA), and the EU AI Act (AIA). Finally, to mitigate identified risks, we provide dual-pronged recommendations that combine regulatory measures and technologi­ cal strategies.
